Retail: 36% of retailers gain at least 10% revenue from AI

In retail, artificial intelligence is no longer just a promise. For some retailers, it already shows up in revenue. According to a global survey of industry professionals conducted in late 2024 and included in Statista's dossier on AI in retail, about 36% of retailers saw AI raise their annual revenue by at least 10%.

The same dossier reports that 95% of retailers consider generative AI a game changer for their industry. Between near-unanimous enthusiasm and concrete results, the gaps remain significant.

The breakdown of gains

The answers break down as follows. 13% of retailers report an AI-driven annual revenue increase of more than 20%. 23% an increase between 10 and 20%. 18% an increase of 5 to 9%. 21% an increase of less than 5%. And 25% see no impact.

The first two groups together make up the 36% of retailers gaining at least 10%. At the other end, a quarter of retailers still see no effect of AI on their sales.

These figures cover 2024 and are based on company statements. They show a trend rather than an exact measurement, but they reveal a clearly divided industry.

Significant investment

The amounts invested match the expectations. According to the same dossier, retailers in the Asia-Pacific region were estimated to have spent about $4.3 billion on AI in 2025, though less than the region's banking sector, which spent almost $7 billion.

In Europe, retail accounted for almost 10% of total spending on AI and generative AI in 2024, making it the second industry behind banking.

Retail is therefore one of the industries betting most on AI. The question is where that money produces the most results.

Why some gain more than others

The retailers getting the best results are not necessarily the ones spending the most. They are often the ones that have linked AI to concrete decisions: which products to promote, which delivery problems to fix, which pain points to remove from the buying journey.

By contrast, AI deployed without a link to daily decisions has little effect on revenue. It produces dashboards nobody uses or content that does not change customer behavior.

The dossier also notes that marketing and sales is the area where retailers use AI most, but that customer service and supply chain are part of the picture too.

In short, spending is not the same as results.

The link to everyday decisions is what turns AI into revenue.

Customers say what holds sales back

One of the most direct sources of extra revenue is often overlooked: what customers say. Product reviews, pre-purchase questions, post-delivery complaints, conversations with customer service. These messages point precisely to what makes people hesitate, what disappoints them and what brings them back.

Automatic language analysis can read all of this feedback and turn it into actions: fixing a misunderstood product page, solving a recurring sizing problem, improving the packaging of an item that often arrives damaged. Each of these fixes has a direct effect on sales and returns.

Our retail and e-commerce page shows several examples of this kind of analysis.

Unlike many AI projects, this one starts with data retailers already collect every day, and produces findings that store, product and customer service teams can act on the same week.

How to get on the right side

For a retailer among the 25% with no visible impact, the first step is not necessarily buying a new tool. It is choosing a precise use, linked to a commercial decision, and measuring its effect over time.

Analyzing reviews and complaints is a good starting point: the data already exists, the results are easy for teams to understand, and the resulting actions can be measured quickly. The models involved are Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case.

Customer data stays hosted in France and is never used to train models.

The takeaway

More than a third of retailers already gain at least 10% revenue from AI, but a quarter see no effect. What makes the difference is the link between AI and concrete decisions. And among those decisions, the ones based on what customers say are often the most profitable.

What this means for you
